TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- For years Ahmad has been unable to find true love. So the 27 year-old bachelor who lives in Tehran is turning to a professional matchmaker. Jafar Ardabili's matchmaking service provides one option for Iranian singles. "I'm searching for a love that lasts," Ahmad said. What's unusual is Ahmad's matchmaker wears a turban, a robe and could be the first-ever Iranian cleric who plays cupid. "First they say 'wow'," Jafar Ardabili said, "then they take a closer look and say 'since he's a cleric we have faith in him.'" Ardabili made his first love match 10 years ago while he taught at a Tehran university. One of his students had a crush on a person, so Ardabili arranged for the two to meet. A few months later they married. The set-up worked so well that Ardabili and his wife opened the Amin International Family and Cultural Institute, a service that matched Iranian singles in a supervised setting. In Iran, Islamic law restricts social interaction. "You can't just go after someone in public and say would you like to live with me?" Ardabili said. "Especially the women, who often don't have any right to choose their companion, but in our institute women do have the right to choose." Ahmad would love nothing more than one of those women to choose him. On a Thursday morning he anxiously sat in the institute's waiting room. Ardabili had arranged for Ahmad to meet a young lady. Could she be the one? Ahmad had paid a $100 fee, submitted a picture and his information. In return he has access to thousands of other applicants. Once applicants approve of one another's pictures and profiles Ardabili arranges up to two meetings inside his office. After each meeting, the applicants report back to Ardabili. "When there's no connection they look like wrinkled potatoes," Ardabili said. And when cupid's arrow hits the mark? "They look very eager. They're as happy as an ice cream cone."  Watch Ardabili describe how his service works » . The third meeting for couples takes place outside the institute without supervision. If all goes well, Ardabili arranges for the families to meet and then the couple ties the knot. "You feel good because you're serving humanity," Ardabili said. Ardabili said that during the past 10 years his institute has had more than 50,000 applicants. More than 2,000 of his couples have married without a single divorce, he said. Ardabili gave credit to his 10-member staff that offers counseling to married couples, even sex therapy. "We want to reduce divorce, give families a strong foundation," Ardabili said. On his Web site, Tehran's matchmaking mullah has posted wedding pictures of some of his success stories. Ahmad can't wait to see his picture among them. "At this very moment I'm counting down the days."

TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- For years, Ahmad has struggled to find true love. Now, at 27, the Tehran bachelor has turned to a professional matchmaker for help. Jafar Ardabili's matchmaking service offers one option among many for Iranian singles seeking companionship. "I'm searching for a love that lasts," Ahmad explained.

What sets Ahmad's matchmaker apart is unusual indeed: Ardabili wears a turban and robe, and may well be Iran's first cleric to play cupid. "First they say, 'Wow,'" Ardabili remarked, "then they take a closer look and say, 'Since he's a cleric, we have faith in him.'"

Ardabili arranged his first successful match a decade ago while teaching at a university in Tehran. One of his students had developed feelings for someone, so Ardabili facilitated an introduction. A few months later, the couple married.

The success of this pairing inspired Ardabili and his wife to establish the Amin International Family and Cultural Institute, a service dedicated to matching Iranian singles in a supervised environment. In Iran, Islamic law places significant restrictions on social interaction between men and women. "You can't simply approach someone in public and ask, 'Would you like to spend your life with me?'" Ardabili said. "This is especially true for women, who often lack the freedom to choose their own companions. At our institute, however, women do have that right."

Ahmad hopes to be chosen by one such woman. On a Thursday morning, he sat anxiously in the institute's waiting room, awaiting a meeting Ardabili had arranged with a young woman. Could she be the one?

Ahmad had paid a $100 fee and submitted a photograph along with his personal information. In exchange, he gained access to a database of thousands of other applicants. Once two applicants express mutual interest based on photographs and profiles, Ardabili arranges up to two supervised meetings in his office. Afterward, each participant reports back on how the encounter went.

"When there's no connection, they look like wrinkled potatoes," Ardabili observed. And when there is a spark? "They look eager—happy as an ice cream cone."

If the first two meetings go well, a third, unsupervised meeting takes place outside the institute. Should everything continue smoothly, Ardabili facilitates an introduction between the couple's families, paving the way toward marriage. "You feel good, because you're serving humanity," he said.

Over the past decade, Ardabili estimates his institute has processed more than 50,000 applications. Of these, over 2,000 couples have married—and, he notes with pride, not a single one has divorced. He credits much of this success to his ten-member staff, who provide ongoing counseling to married couples, including guidance on intimacy. "We want to reduce divorce and give families a strong foundation," Ardabili said.

On his website, Tehran's matchmaking mullah proudly displays wedding photographs from some of his many success stories. Ahmad is eager to see his own photo added to the collection. "At this very moment," he said, "I'm counting down the days."

TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- Ahmad, 27, has spent years searching unsuccessfully for genuine romance in the Iranian capital. Now this single man has decided to enlist professional help—Jafar Ardabili, a matchmaker who offers Tehran's unmarried residents an alternative path to romance. "What I'm looking for is love that endures," Ahmad explained. The unusual twist here is that Ahmad's matchmaker dresses in traditional clerical garb—turban and robe included—potentially making him Iran's first religious figure to take on the role of matchmaker. According to Ardabili, "People's initial reaction is surprise. Then they look more carefully and realize, 'Because he's a member of the clergy, we can trust him.'"

Ardabili's career as a matchmaker began ten years back when he was teaching at a university in Tehran. A student confided in him about romantic feelings for someone, prompting Ardabili to facilitate an introduction. Marriage followed within months. This success inspired Ardabili and his spouse to establish the Amin International Family and Cultural Institute—an organization dedicated to connecting single Iranians under proper supervision.

Islamic law in Iran places significant limits on interactions between men and women. As Ardabili put it, "Public pursuit of romantic interest isn't an option—you simply cannot approach someone and propose cohabitation directly." He added that women face particular restrictions, often lacking any say in choosing partners. "Our institute, however, gives women that choice."

Being chosen is exactly what Ahmad hopes for. He waited nervously in the institute's reception area one Thursday morning, having been scheduled to meet a potential match. Was she the one he'd been seeking? Ahmad had already paid $100, provided a photograph, and submitted his personal details—gaining access, in exchange, to a database containing thousands of other hopefuls.

The process works like this: once two people express mutual interest based on photos and profiles, Ardabili organizes as many as two supervised meetings within his office. Following each encounter, participants provide feedback. Ardabili has learned to read the signs. "Lack of chemistry shows on their faces—they end up looking like shriveled potatoes," he noted. But genuine attraction produces a different reaction entirely. "You can tell—they're practically glowing with excitement, delighted like kids holding ice cream cones."

Should a couple progress past the initial supervised sessions, a third meeting happens independently, without institute oversight. Assuming things continue smoothly, Ardabili then brings the two families together, paving the way toward marriage. "There's real satisfaction in knowing you're contributing something meaningful to society," he reflected.

Over the past decade, Ardabili estimates his institute has processed applications from over 50,000 people. Among these, more than 2,000 couples have wed—and remarkably, none have divorced, according to Ardabili. He attributes part of this success to his staff of ten, who provide ongoing counseling services to married couples, including guidance on sexual matters. "Lowering divorce rates and building solid family foundations—that's our goal," he said.

The institute's website showcases wedding photographs celebrating these matchmaking triumphs. Ahmad is eager to eventually see his own photo featured there. "Right now," he said, "I'm just counting down the days."

# Finding Love Through Tradition: The Rise of Clerical Matchmaking in Iran

In the bustling city of Tehran, 27-year-old Ahmad represents a growing number of young Iranians turning to professional matchmaking services in their quest for lasting companionship. As a bachelor navigating the complexities of modern romance within a traditional society, Ahmad has found that seeking assistance through structured, supervised introductions offers a practical path toward marriage—one that honors cultural and religious sensitivities while still allowing for personal choice.

At the center of this matchmaking movement stands Jafar Ardabili, a figure whose career represents a unique intersection of faith and modern service. Ardabili holds the distinction of being, quite possibly, the first Iranian cleric to take on the role of professional matchmaker. This unconventional path merges his religious credentials and moral authority with a practical, hands-on approach to helping young people find spouses—an unusual pairing that has nonetheless found considerable acceptance and success within Iranian society.

The origins of Ardabili's matchmaking career trace back roughly a decade, to when he successfully arranged a union between two university students. Encouraged by this early success, Ardabili and his wife went on to establish the Amin International Family and Cultural Institute, formalizing what began as an informal act of goodwill into a structured, ongoing service. Since then, the institute has grown into a recognized resource for those seeking marriage partners through a process rooted in both tradition and careful oversight.

The service fills an important social need in Iran, where Islamic law imposes significant restrictions on unsupervised interaction between unmarried men and women. In this context, Ardabili's institute offers a sanctioned alternative, creating a safe and religiously appropriate framework within which potential partners can meet. Notably, the service places particular emphasis on empowering women, granting them agency and the right to choose among potential suitors—a meaningful development in a society where such choices have not always been readily available to women.

The matchmaking process itself is methodical and deliberate. Prospective clients begin by paying an application fee and submitting detailed personal profiles, which Ardabili uses to identify potentially compatible matches. Once a promising pairing is identified, the two individuals are permitted up to two supervised meetings, held within the confines of Ardabili's own office. These meetings serve not only as opportunities for the applicants to get to know one another but also as a means for Ardabili to assess compatibility firsthand. By carefully observing the reactions and demeanor of both parties following each meeting, he is able to gauge whether a genuine connection has formed—insight that ultimately informs his guidance on whether the match should move forward toward marriage.

Through this blend of religious authority, personal experience, and structured process, Ardabili's institute has carved out a distinctive niche in Iranian society—one that respects longstanding cultural and religious boundaries while adapting to the evolving needs of a new generation seeking love and lasting partnership.

# The Cleric's Matchmaking Revolution: How One Tehran Institute is Redefining Courtship in Iran

In a modest office tucked away in central Tehran, an unlikely figure has emerged as a champion of romantic connection in a society where the simple act of a man and woman talking in public can invite scrutiny, suspicion, or worse. Jafar Ardabili, a Muslim cleric by training and vocation, has spent years building something that might seem contradictory at first glance: a matchmaking institute that operates within the strict boundaries of Islamic law while still managing to help thousands of Iranian singles find companionship, and in many cases, marriage.

Ardabili's approach is as pragmatic as it is innovative. Recognizing that Iranian law and cultural norms severely restrict unsupervised or unofficial interactions between unmarried men and women, he has created a system where the initial stages of courtship happen not through chance encounters or forbidden clandestine meetings, but through a carefully curated process that begins with paperwork and photographs rather than stolen glances across a crowded room.

At the heart of his institute lies an extensive database, thousands of profiles deep, containing information about hopeful singles from across the city and beyond. Men and women who come to Ardabili seeking partners are given the opportunity to browse through these profiles, examining photographs, reading about backgrounds, professions, family values, and personal interests, before ever laying eyes on a potential match in person. This screening process, conducted in a manner that satisfies religious and legal requirements, allows participants to exercise a degree of choice and agency that might otherwise be unavailable to them.

This is particularly significant for the women who seek out Ardabili's services. In a society where women often have limited control over their romantic prospects, where family introductions and arranged circumstances frequently dictate the course of their marital futures, the ability to actively select from a pool of potential suitors represents a meaningful shift in agency. Rather than waiting passively for a match to be arranged by relatives or acquaintances, women who come to Ardabili's institute can take an active role in identifying qualities and characteristics they find appealing, narrowing down candidates based on their own preferences and priorities.

Once initial interest is established through the profile review process, Ardabili's institute facilitates supervised meetings between the prospective couple. These encounters are carefully structured to comply with Islamic guidelines governing interaction between unrelated men and women, ensuring that the budding relationship develops within an acceptable framework while still allowing the individuals involved to genuinely get to know one another.

The results speak to the effectiveness of this unconventional approach. Among the institute's success stories is Ahmad, one of many clients who found a marriage partner through Ardabili's careful matchmaking process. Ahmad's experience mirrors that of numerous others who have walked through the doors of this Tehran institute, uncertain about how to navigate the complex terrain of finding a spouse in a society with such stringent social restrictions, only to emerge with a partner selected through a process that honored both their personal preferences and their religious obligations.

What makes Ardabili's institute particularly noteworthy is its position at the intersection of tradition and modernity. By leveraging a systematic, almost bureaucratic approach to matchmaking, complete with extensive databases and structured profiles, he has essentially created a solution that satisfies conservative religious requirements while still providing something akin to the choice and agency that dating services in other parts of the world offer. It represents a distinctly Iranian solution to a distinctly Iranian challenge, one that acknowledges the constraints of the legal and religious framework while still working within it to serve a fundamental human need: the desire for connection, companionship, and marriage.

As word of the institute's success spreads, it stands as a testament to the kind of pragmatic innovation that can emerge even within the most restrictive of social frameworks, offering a glimpse of how tradition and the very human desire for choice in matters of the heart can find common ground.

Recent developments have drawn scrutiny from Western powers, with CNN and other international news outlets providing extensive coverage of the situation from both Tehran and various global capitals.

counterfactuals.output:
# In Tehran, a Cleric Turns Matchmaker for the Faithful and the Frustrated

**TEHRAN** — In a modest office tucked behind a mosque in central Tehran, Sheikh Hossein Mahdavi doesn't just offer religious guidance — he offers something many young Iranians say is harder to find: a spouse.

Three days a week, the 52-year-old cleric trades his role as a preacher for that of a matchmaker, running what he calls a "marriage counseling service" that has quietly become one of the most sought-after ways for religiously observant singles to meet in a country where dating apps are officially banned and social mixing between unmarried men and women remains fraught with cultural and legal risk.

"Marriage is half of faith, according to our Prophet," Mahdavi said, sitting behind a desk stacked with manila folders — each one a profile of a hopeful client. "But young people today don't know how to find their other half. The old ways have broken down, and the new ways are forbidden or distrusted. I'm just filling the gap."

## A Growing Need

Iran's marriage rate has fallen sharply over the past decade, a trend officials have linked to economic hardship, delayed financial independence among young adults, and changing social attitudes. Government surveys show the average age of first marriage has crept upward, alarming clerical and political leaders who see the trend as a threat to traditional family structures.

In response, mosques, cultural centers, and state-backed organizations across Iran have rolled out matchmaking initiatives — some organized through official "marriage exhibitions," others more informal, like Mahdavi's.

His service works something like an old-fashioned marriage bureau crossed with a confidential dating pool. Applicants — he says he has helped more than 1,200 people over eight years — fill out lengthy questionnaires covering their education, religious observance, career, financial situation, and family expectations. Mahdavi and a small team of assistants, including his wife, review profiles and suggest potential matches, often arranging supervised meetings in the mosque's reception hall or a nearby restaurant.

"We are very careful," Mahdavi said. "Families are involved from the beginning. This is not like the applications on phones. There is no secrecy, no games."

## Skepticism and Support

Not everyone in Tehran is convinced clerical matchmaking is the answer to the country's marriage slump. Sociologists point out that economic pressures — inflation, unemployment, and soaring housing costs — remain the primary obstacles keeping young Iranians from marrying, regardless of how they meet.

"You can introduce a hundred couples, but if the man can't afford rent and the woman doesn't trust the economy enough to plan a future, matchmaking won't fix that," said Elham Bagheri, a sociologist at a Tehran research institute who studies family trends.

Still, for some clients, the service has offered something dating apps and family networks could not.

Narges, a 29-year-old pharmacist who asked that her last name be withheld, said she came to Mahdavi after years of resisting family pressure to marry through traditional introductions arranged by relatives.

"My aunt kept introducing me to men who wanted a housewife, not a partner," she said. "Sheikh Mahdavi actually listened to what I wanted in a career and in a marriage. He didn't just look at appearances or family reputation."

She married a man she met through the service last year.

## Faith Meets Practicality

Mahdavi insists his work isn't really about romance — it's about restoring what he sees as a religious and social obligation increasingly abandoned by modern life. He often quotes verses on the importance of marriage during his Friday sermons, using the pulpit to recruit both clients and volunteers to help run the service.

He acknowledges the criticism that clerics have no business playing matchmaker, and that his approach — however well-intentioned — cannot solve Iran's deeper demographic and economic challenges.

"I am not an economist. I cannot lower the price of an apartment," he said. "But I can bring two lonely people into the same room and let God do the rest."

As he spoke, an assistant knocked on the door with a new folder: a 34-year-old engineer, recently returned from working abroad, looking for a wife who "understands ambition." Mahdavi smiled, added it to the growing stack, and got back to work.

counterfactuals.output:
# The Matchmaker of Isfahan

Zahra Moradi's office isn't really an office—it's the front room of her modest apartment near the Si-o-se-pol bridge, where she's placed two facing couches and a small table that's always set with tea and dates. For ninely-three years, this room has been the site of countless first conversations, hesitant confessions, and, so far, forty-one marriages.

"People think what I do is old-fashioned," she says, laughing as she pours tea for a young man who arrived twenty minutes early for his appointment, sitting nervously with his hands folded. "But everyone who comes through that door is using an app on their phone the whole time they wait to see me."

Zahra became a matchmaker—an *khواستگار* in the traditional sense, though she prefers to just be called "Auntie Zahra" by her clients—after her own daughter's marriage fell apart from what she calls "the loneliness of modern searching." Dating apps exist in Iran, technically operating in gray areas, but many families still prefer someone who understands not just compatibility, but the specific texture of a religious life: how someone prays, whether they fast completely during Ramadan, how they think about raising children in the faith.

"A person can lie in a bio," she says. "They cannot lie to me for three meetings while I watch how they treat their mother on the phone."

Her method is unhurried. She meets separately with families first, understanding their expectations, their flexibility, their fears. Then she arranges supervised meetings—usually with a family member present, in accordance with religious guidelines about unmarried men and women interacting. Some families are strict; others, especially in the cities, want more space for the couple to simply talk.

Maryam, twenty-six, an engineering graduate, came to Zahra after her family grew anxious about her age. "I wanted someone who prayed like I prayed—not performing it, but actually believing it," she says. "But I also didn't want someone who would tell me I couldn't work after marriage."

Zahra found her a match in Hossein, an accountant with a quiet sense of humor and a mother who, refreshingly, wanted a daughter-in-law with her own career. They married eight months ago.

Not every match succeeds. Zahra keeps a small notebook of "near-misses"—couples who met, respected each other, but felt no warmth. She doesn't consider these failures. "Better to know before the contract than after," she says.

She charges very little, mostly gifts of sweets or fabric, though families sometimes insist on money. What she really wants, she says, is not payment but attendance at the weddings.

"I sit in the back," she says. "I don't need to be at the front. I just want to see their faces when they finally look at each other and know."

Outside, the call to prayer drifts over the rooftops, and Zahra glances at her watch—another family is arriving in ten minutes, hopeful, uncertain, trusting her eye for finding what algorithms, they believe, cannot.

# In Tehran's Marriage Market, a Mullah Trades Sermons for Speed-Dating

**TEHRAN** — On Thursday evenings, when the call to prayer fades from the loudspeakers near his mosque in central Tehran, Sheikh Ali Reza Moghaddam swaps his role as spiritual guide for something he never anticipated in his years of seminary study: professional matchmaker.

In a modest reception hall behind his mosque, rows of folding chairs face each other, occupied by nervous young men on one side and their families sizing up prospects on the other. It's not a wedding — not yet, anyway. It's what Moghaddam has come to call "Thursday Nights," a matchmaking service that has quietly grown from a favor for a neighbor's son into a operation serving hundreds of Tehran's unmarried faithful.

"People used to come to me only for religious rulings — is this food halal, is this business permissible," Moghaddam said, adjusting his turban as he reviewed a stack of handwritten profiles. "Now they come to me and say, 'Sheikh, find me a wife.' I tell them, marriage is also a religious matter. Perhaps the most important one."

Iran's marriage rates have declined steadily over the past decade, according to the country's National Organization for Civil Registration, with economic pressures, delayed education, and shifting social attitudes cited as key factors. Sociologists have noted that fewer young Iranians are meeting through traditional family networks, creating an opening that some clerics — attuned to community needs — have stepped in to fill.

Moghaddam insists he never set out to become what local media have dubbed "the marrying mullah."

"A widow in my congregation asked me to help her son, who was too shy to find a wife on his own," he said. "I made one match. Then another. Now I have a waiting list longer than my Friday sermon."

His method blends old and new: prospective matches fill out questionnaires covering religious observance, education, family background, and — increasingly — compatibility questions borrowed loosely from psychology.

"I ask them: What do you want from life? Do you pray together as important, or is it enough that God is in your heart? These things matter more than a good job or a beautiful face, though of course," he added, smiling, "those things do not hurt."

## A Client's Perspective

Among those who found success through Moghaddam's sessions is Ahmad Karimi, a 29-year-old engineer from Tehran's Nazi-Abad district, who met his fiancée at one of the Thursday gatherings six months ago.

"I was embarrassed at first," Ahmad admitted, sitting in a tea house near his workplace. "My mother suggested it, and I thought, this is something for older, more traditional families. But everyone at university is busy, everyone at work is busy. Where else was I supposed to meet someone serious about marriage?"

Ahmad said what struck him most was the sheikh's directness. "He doesn't waste time with small talk. He looked at my profile and said, 'I think I know someone for you, but she wants a husband who will support her continuing her studies. Is this acceptable to you?' I said yes. Two weeks later, I met Zahra."

The couple plans to marry in the spring. "My grandmother keeps telling everyone the mullah performed a miracle," Ahmad laughed. "I tell her, no miracle — just organization. He's like a very religious dating app, except he actually calls you back."

## Balancing Tradition and Modern Life

Not everyone in Tehran's clerical establishment has embraced Moghaddam's approach. Some traditionalists argue that matchmaking should remain a family affair, not a service run from a mosque annex with — as one local newspaper noted — a growing social media following where Moghaddam posts anonymized success stories.

Moghaddam is unbothered by the criticism.

"The Prophet, peace be upon him, helped his companions find spouses. Is this not the same principle? Times change. The mechanism changes. But the goal — building strong families, reducing loneliness, preventing sin — this never changes."

He estimates he has facilitated more than 150 marriages in the past three years, though he keeps no official records "out of respect for people's privacy."

As dusk settled over Tehran and the Thursday session drew to a close, Moghaddam moved between the rows of chairs, offering tea and quiet words of encouragement to families still negotiating the delicate dance of introduction.

"Every match is different," he said. "But every person deserves someone who makes their life easier, not harder. This is not just paperwork for me. This is worship."

For Ahmad, at least, the sheikh's unconventional service delivered on its promise.

"People think finding a wife through a mullah sounds old-fashioned," he said. "But honestly? It felt more modern than anything else I tried."

*This feature is a fictional composite created for illustrative purposes.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

# Tehran Matchmaker Blends Faith and Romance in Search for Perfect Match

**TEHRAN, Iran (CNN)** — In a modest office building in central Tehran, Sheikh Hossein Ansari-Rad shuffles through stacks of handwritten applications, each one representing someone's hope for love. Known locally as the "matchmaking mullah," the 52-year-old cleric has spent the past decade building one of Iran's most unconventional marriage institutes — one that fuses religious tradition with practical, almost clinical, matchmaking.

"Marriage is half of faith," Ansari-Rad said, quoting a well-known Islamic saying, as he adjusted his black turban and gestured to the filing cabinets lining his walls. "But faith alone doesn't put food on the table or raise children well. We look at everything."

## From Seminary to Matrimony

Ansari-Rad trained for nearly 15 years at the Qom seminary, Iran's preeminent center of Shiite religious scholarship, before deciding his true calling lay not in issuing religious edicts, but in solving what he calls "the loneliness crisis" facing Iran's young and middle-aged singles.

"I saw so many families come to me for advice, and always it came back to the same problem — good, honest people who simply could not find each other," he said. He founded the Institute for Righteous Union in 2013, initially operating out of a single room in a mosque annex. Today, the institute claims more than 3,000 active files and says it has facilitated over 800 marriages.

## Strict Rules, Careful Vetting

The institute's methods are notably rigorous. Applicants — men and women alike — must submit detailed questionnaires covering income, education, health records, family background, and religious observance. A committee of three, including Ansari-Rad himself, reviews each file before any potential match is proposed.

"We do not simply pair people by age or by looks," Ansari-Rad said. "We ask: What kind of household will these two build together? Will their families accept the union? Are their expectations realistic?"

Candidates are required to meet for a minimum of three chaperoned sessions before any decision is made, and financial transparency is mandatory — a rule Ansari-Rad insists prevents future disputes. Men must disclose their salary and housing situation; women must state clearly whether they intend to work after marriage.

"Some people find this old-fashioned," he acknowledged. "But we have very few divorces among our matches. Less than five percent, by my count."

## Ahmad's Search

Among those hoping the sheikh's system will work is Ahmad Karimi, a 34-year-old auto parts salesman from the working-class Nazi-Abad district of southern Tehran.

Ahmad has been registered with the institute for eight months and has met four women through its process — so far, without success.

"The first one, we had nothing to talk about," he said, laughing somewhat ruefully in the institute's waiting room, worry beads moving through his fingers. "The second, her family wanted too much for the dowry. I am not a rich man."

Ahmad said he turned to Ansari-Rad's institute after growing frustrated with Iran's booming but, in his view, unreliable matchmaking apps, which have proliferated despite periodic government crackdowns on unmarried men and women mixing.

"On the apps, you don't know who is real," he said. "Here, at least, Sheikh Ansari-Rad has met these women's families. There is trust."

Ahmad said he is looking for a wife who is "practical, kind, and not obsessed with appearances" — and one who will tolerate his long hours at the shop he hopes to eventually own outright.

Ansari-Rad said he believes he may have found a promising match for Ahmad: a 29-year-old kindergarten teacher from the nearby Molavi district, whose file, he said, "shows patience, and family stability — the two things Ahmad needs most."

The two are scheduled to meet for the first time next week, under the watchful, hopeful eye of the matchmaking mullah himself.

"In the end," Ansari-Rad said, closing Ahmad's file with a satisfied nod, "we are not just matching two people. We are trying to build a foundation for society, one household at a time."
